explanations.explanation: That's the promise, baker. The writer says, "I will praise the LORD all my life; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being." (Psalm 146:2) No expiration date and no fine print. I wish I'd kept promises that well, because I once swore I'd only eat ONE broken cookie per batch.

I get why that sounds right, friend, since lots of folks only sing when life is smooth. But the writer doesn't put a condition on it. He says, "I will praise the LORD all my life…" (Psalm 146:2) Troubles never get a vote.

Feast days are a nice guess, baker, but the psalm never mentions them. The writer says he'll praise the LORD "all my life," and he'll sing praises "while I have my being." (Psalm 146:2) That covers feast days AND the boring Tuesdays in between.

Yep, that's what it says. "Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save." (Psalm 146:3) Princes are impressive, but the psalm calls them mortal men. Trust placed there has nothing to hold it up.

This one is true, friend. The psalm says, "Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save." (Psalm 146:3) The warning is aimed at princes, and it names them as mortal men who cannot save. The fancy title doesn't change that.

This is the opposite of what the psalm says, baker. It says, "When his spirit departs, he returns to the ground; on that very day his plans perish." (Psalm 146:4) The plans don't live on. They perish the same day.
That's right. The psalm says his plans perish "on that very day." (Psalm 146:4) The man returns to the ground, and his plans go with him. Nobody gets to take a masterplan into the next day.

That's it, friend. "Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God." (Psalm 146:5) Help and hope land in the same place. Jacob was Israel's forefather, so this is the God of a long family line.
I know, we all like to lean on ourselves, and I've tried it plenty. But the psalm says the blessed one's hope "is in the LORD his God." (Psalm 146:5) His own strength never makes the list.

Good deeds are a fine thing, baker, but they aren't where this hope sits. The psalm says the blessed one's help is "the God of Jacob," and his hope "is in the LORD his God." (Psalm 146:5) The hope is in a Person, not a pile of deeds.
Not quite, friend. The psalm says of the LORD, "He remains faithful forever." (Psalm 146:6) There's no "if" attached to it, and no condition on His people. Forever means forever.

Right. The psalm says, "He remains faithful forever." (Psalm 146:6) It doesn't say "as long as," and it doesn't hang His faithfulness on anyone else. Compare that to the princes in verse 3, whose plans end the day they do.
There it is, baker. "He executes justice for the oppressed." (Psalm 146:7) It's the first thing on the list, and the very next thing is food for the hungry. The oppressed are first in line.
New land sounds like a big, generous answer, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The psalm says, "He executes justice for the oppressed." (Psalm 146:7) Justice is what the oppressed get.

Interesting guess, baker, but the psalm never says that. It says, "He executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry." (Psalm 146:7) Justice is the first thing on the list, and no thrones are mentioned.
Yes! "The LORD sets the prisoners free." (Psalm 146:7) It comes right after the food for the hungry. Friend, that line gets me every single time.
Not the wealthy, baker. The psalm says, "The LORD sets the prisoners free." (Psalm 146:7) Notice who is on this list: the oppressed, the hungry and the prisoners.
I see why you'd pick that, friend, but the proud don't show up in this line. It says, "The LORD sets the prisoners free." (Psalm 146:7) Prisoners are the ones getting freed here.
You got it, baker. "The LORD loves the righteous." (Psalm 146:8) That line sits right after He opens the eyes of the blind and lifts those weighed down. It's all one long list of what He does.
The mighty are an easy guess, friend, since power gets a lot of attention. But the psalm says, "the LORD loves the righteous." (Psalm 146:8) The mighty are never named as the ones He loves.
Fame gets a ton of attention, baker, but not here. The psalm says, "the LORD loves the righteous." (Psalm 146:8) The famous never make the list.

That's right, friend. The psalm says, "but the ways of the wicked He frustrates." (Psalm 146:9) Everything before it in the verse was about the LORD caring for foreigners, the fatherless and the widow. Then comes the turn.
That's not what the psalm says, baker. It says, "the ways of the wicked He frustrates." (Psalm 146:9) So He does something about their ways, and leaving them alone isn't it.
Close the book on that one, friend. The psalm says the opposite: "the ways of the wicked He frustrates." (Psalm 146:9) Their ways get frustrated, not prospered.
That's the last line, baker. "The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations." (Psalm 146:10) Forever, and for all generations. Princes come and go, but this reign doesn't end.

"For now" is what you'd say about a prince, friend, and the psalm already told us how that goes in verse 4. About the LORD it says, "The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations." (Psalm 146:10) Nothing temporary about it.
Decades is a long time, baker, but it's still too short. The psalm says, "The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations." (Psalm 146:10) Forever has no countdown on it.
